sm: Host Georgia Howe opens the Friday, November 20th Evening Wire, with John Bickley out on vacation. The top story is Poland accusing Russia of intentional provocation after missile strikes reached its territory. During an overnight offensive of around 400 drones and over 100 missiles launched at Ukraine, some reportedly landed in Poland or entered its airspace. Russia says this and earlier incidents were unintentional, but Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said what landed came from Russia and does not look like an accident, a view he says NATO partners share. The strikes in Ukraine also hit the Austrian embassy and nearly hit the Netherlands embassy, so France called an emergency UN Security Council meeting. Incursions into NATO member Poland pose a dilemma for allies, including the United States.

The Trump administration's national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, is stepping down soon. According to Axios, he wants to leave now so the Senate can confirm a replacement before Democrats take control of the chamber next year. Kirsten Davies, currently the Chief Information Officer at the War Department, will replace him. She is said to have more experience with tech and AI, and she has already been Senate confirmed. It is unclear whether she will stay or hold the job temporarily. His exit follows a week of tech outages in the private sector and government, which officials blamed on glitches rather than malicious attacks.

The Senate advanced a landmark permitting reform bill on Thursday, meant to streamline approval of large energy and infrastructure projects. After more than a year of haggling that stalled as elections neared, a coalition of Democrats joined Republicans to pass the American Affordability and Jobs Act, 62 to 33. It still needs House approval before reaching President Trump. Separately, a stock market sell-off has bruised investors this month. Anthropic's record-setting IPO on Thursday did not stop the slide, and its stock dropped 10 percent after an initial surge. The S&P fell more than 6 percent over the week, its worst in over a year, and the Nasdaq fell over 3 percent. Investors appear to have lost confidence in AI, and the scandal over ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has hurt trust further. Nvidia's losses make up roughly half of the 8 percent S&P drop since early October.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's decision to ban horse-drawn carriages in Central Park has drawn a lawsuit from carriage drivers. The Transportation Workers Union filed suit yesterday, arguing the pending ban is unconstitutional and that the city violated legal procedure in passing it. The ban was largely spurred by the publicized death of a teenage boy earlier this year, who was thrown from a carriage by a spooked horse. Animal rights activists have long sought such a ban. Drivers say the mayor has denied them their livelihood and destroyed a historic institution. Mamdani defended the move, saying the city has changed and its laws should too.

Daily Wire editor Zach Jewell reports on the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in northern Africa, which has been plagued by crime since tens of thousands of migrants crossed in from Morocco. An estimated 70,000 to 80,000 people rushed the border in late July. According to Spanish media, since then there have been six times as many sexual assaults reported, seven times as many firearm attacks and twelve times as many knife attacks. Police have struggled to clear homeless camps that have appeared across the city and strained municipal resources. The Spanish government has promised to deport the migrants, but thousands are reportedly still in the city.

A 4.2 magnitude earthquake rattled the Los Angeles area early Friday, with shaking reported as far as 115 miles away. It struck near Commerce, about seven miles southeast of downtown. Mayor Karen Bass reported no immediate damage or disruptions, including at LAX, and the fire department reported no significant structural damage or injuries. In Virginia, a school district closed all 29 of its schools through Thanksgiving after finding that more than 500 employees hired over three years were never screened against the state's child abuse and neglect registry. They had passed criminal background checks, but staff responsible for the extra screenings failed to follow procedures. Acting superintendent Chandra Hayes said no related investigations or charges were found. Staff working with children must complete screenings first, an outside investigation is planned, and schools should reopen November 30th.

Fourteen people have been charged in a Southern California train robbery ring accused of stealing more than 22.5 million dollars in consumer goods over two years. Lifestyle reporter Lauren Baer says federal prosecutors allege the group targeted freight trains between February 2024 and August 2026, sometimes forcing emergency stops before loading stolen sneakers, power tools and other merchandise into trucks and vans. The cargo went to stash houses and was resold on the black market. The youngest defendant, 21, allegedly led the operation, with 13 co-conspirators. All face conspiracy and cargo theft charges, plus counts of violence against railroad carriers, which carry up to life in federal prison.

Amid a rise in anti-Semitic attacks, Alliance Defending Freedom senior counsel Andrew Spanberger explains that a Maryland synagogue is challenging a county ban. Silver Spring Jewish Center is asking the Fourth Circuit to block a Montgomery County ordinance, enacted in July, banning firearms inside and within 100 yards of places of public assembly, including houses of worship. Hired guards are exempt, as are permit holders passing through by car. A federal district court blocked the ban inside the synagogue but left the 100-yard zone, so congregants can carry inside but not on the walk there, which matters because they walk to services on the Sabbath and holidays. The synagogue cites growing threats since October 7th, 2023, including an assault outside and an attempted break-in. Beckett's Eric Baxter, who represents it, says this is no protection at all. The host then closes the show, noting earlier coverage of President Trump's Asia trip, a senator on online threats to children from gaming platforms, and record Grand Theft Auto 6 sales.
sg: Carriage ban lawsuit in New York
Los Angeles quake and Virginia schools
